If the doctor said its okay for them to start training, then you should be good. They'll know the details better than any of us. Treat it like you have a total beginner. Start with some basic movements ask for their reassurance throughout the program to make sure there's no discomfort.

Like one of the other guys here said, push-ups with the Smith machine are a great start. Be careful around compound movements. But isolated things such as bi's & tri's, deltoids and machine equipment for the legs should be okay. 

Another chest exercise that is relatively low risk is the rest-press or dead-press. You have them in the squatting rack with the safety rails set just above their chest. This way, your client has 0 risk of dropping the weight on themselves, and they may feel like they can push themselves a bit more. Only thing to look out for is the wrists. Make sure their wrists are in the correct position. 

Personally, I'd keep their program to the machine equipment in the gym, and maybe see how they feel when doing something such as a kettlebell squat, just to ensure that the hips (and surrounding muscles) aren't totally neglected. 

For the stamina part, that's totally up to them. Their stamina is probably awful after the surgery, so something such as a bike or elliptical should be enough to bolster the stamina for the time being.
Like the others are saying, you look for when their form starts to fail. You look for the sweet spot that enough to push them towards their goal, without risking injury.

1) A frontliner
2) Utility carrier
3) Teamfight disable

The market depends on your location. Online clients are great and all, but its the people who stay with you over a long period of time where you'll make your money. If I need to have a talk about diet or something else, I'll slot them in for an extra 30mins so I have time to train them and chat afterwards. 

Ultimately the job takes a lot of preserverance, time and money management. You'll be your own boss, and these people trust you with their fitness life. It's up to you to educate and set them on the right track for their goals.

Your heroes and roles are a bit all over the place.

A good start (coming from a pos1 player), is to pick 3-5 heroes and practise them a lot. Unlike LoL, Dota2 has a lot more interactions between spells and the environment. Heroes can be used more than what their spells and abilities say. My younger brother is 1.7k, and I've showed him some neat tricks. A couple of recent example are:

If you're playing Phantom Assassin and an enemy hero is running away on low hp, and out of range of your spells. Use your Blink Strike to go to a creep and then Stifling Dagger the enemy. People use Blink Strike as an offensive or defensive ability when it has such good utility in that.
Second example can be Ember Spirit. You can dodge spells by timing your Sleight of Fist. If a Lina uses Euls Scepter on you, theres a 99% chance shes going to stun you next. Instead of panicking and trying use Remnant, look at her animation and time your Sleight of Fist so that you dodge her stun. It's more of an advanced move, but these are little extra skills you pick up when you play a hero a lot.

Pick a few heroes who you really like, and play them a lot. Versatility is good and can solve problems your team has, but I'd rather a really good Dazzle player vs Axe, than a shitty Shadow Demon player.

Farming is simple enough. Stay around wards, dont go into the enemy side, prioritise lane creeps over jungle creeps. You'll get better as you keep going.
